author: catherine-booth
fields.title: Godliness
fields.description: What does true Godliness look like? Discover the transforming power of genuine repentance, living faith, fervent prayer, holy love, and wholehearted surrender to God. Confront counterfeit Christianity, examine your heart in the light of Scripture, and embrace a life marked by holiness, obedience, and spiritual power.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
The sermons of Mrs. Booth already re-published under the title of " Aggressive Christianity ," came to American Christians as a tonic to their weakness, and a stimulant to their inertness.

The sermons in the present volume are a much-needed prophylactic, a safeguard against several practical errors in dealing with souls; errors which lead them into Egyptian darkness, instead of the marvelous light.

The sermon on Repentance is a most faithful showing up of spurious repentance, the vain substitute for a downright abandonment of every form of sin, and right-about facing towards the Lord. In directness and point, it is a model for earnest revival preaching,—rather, for all preaching to unsaved souls, outside the church, or within it. All of these will be found in some subterfuge, which must be ruthlessly torn down, before it will be abandoned for the cleft Rock.

The sermon on Saving Faith is next in order. The disastrous consequences of what, for the want of a better description, maybe styled an Antinomian faith, an unrepentant assent of the intellect to the historic facts of the Gospel, which too many evangelists and other religious teachers are calling saving faith, are clearly set forth and plainly labeled, POISON. This spurious trust in Christ following a superficial repentance, which has never felt the desperate sinfulness and real misery of sin, has furnished our churches with a numerous class of members, aptly described by the prophet Micah: "The sin of Israel is great and unrepented of, yet they will lean on the Lord, and say, Is not the Lord among us?" We are convinced that much of the work of the faithful and pungent preacher, who preaches with his eye fixed on the great white throne and the descending Judge, is to dislodge professors from their imaginary trust in a Saviour who does not save them, and probe deeply their hearts festering with sin, which have been hastily pronounced healed, "slightly healed."

Many of us have incautiously said to awakened souls, "Only believe," before we have thrust the heart through and through with the sword of God's law. We have dismissed God's schoolmaster.

The law, like the slave charged with the task of leading the boy to school, and of committing him to the teacher, we have thought to be too harsh and severe for our sentimental age, and have unwisely discharged, and have assumed its office of a paidagogos to Christ, and we have missed the way, and misled a priceless soul. God have mercy on us, and give us humility, as He gave Apollos, to be set right by an anointed woman!

After her timely correction of erroneous teachings on faith, Mrs. Booth proceeds, pruning-knife in hand, to cut away from the tree of modern Christianity the poisonous fungus of a "spurious love."

Her four sermons on love are four beacons set on the rocks of counterfeit Christian love. She sets forth several infallible tests by which genuine love may be distinguished from the devil's base imitation. Like the Epistles of St. John, these sermons are full of touchstones for testing love, that golden principle of the Christian life. It would be very profitable for all professors of that perfect love which casts out all tormenting fear, to apply unflinchingly these touch-stones to themselves.

They may find the word "perfection" taking on a meaning deeper, broader and higher than they had ever before conceived. Why should not our conception of Christian perfection steadily grow with the increase of our knowledge of God and of His holy law?

The sermon on The Conditions of Effectual Prayer , we commend to all Christians and to all seekers of Christ, who are mourning because their prayers do not prevail with God. In the clear light of this sermon they will find that the difficulty lies, either in the lack of fellowship with Jesus Christ, or of obedience to His commands, or in the absence from their hearts of the interceding Spirit, or in defective faith. In the discussion of these hindrances to prayer, the preacher lays open the heart, and with a skilful spiritual surgery, searches it to the very bottom. The incisiveness of her style, her courage and plain dealing with her hearers, tearing off the masks of sin and selfishness, the various guises in which these masquerade in many Christian hearts and obstruct their access to a throne of grace, remind us of Dr. Finney's unsparing exposure and condemnation of these enemies to Christian holiness, and of John Wesley's cutting up by the roots "Sin in Believers."

In this sermon, Mrs. Booth turns her attention to another phase of faith and of practical error in the guidance of souls to Christ. Her views on this vexed question are not extreme but philosophical and scriptural. She teaches that God has made the bestowment of salvation simultaneous with the exercise of faith, and that "telling a person to believe he is saved, before he is saved, is telling him to believe a lie." But she insists that the act of faith is put forth with the special aid of the Holy Spirit giving an assurance that the blessing sought will be granted. This assurance, or earnest, given by the Spirit, becomes the basis on which the final act of faith rests, namely, "I believe that I receive." This corresponds with William Taylor's Divine "ascertainment of the fact of the sinner's surrender to God, and his acceptance of Christ," before justification. [Footnote: Election of Grace, pp. 38-42.] Both teachers agree with Wesley's analysis of faith which teaches that the fourth and last step, "He doth it," can be taken only by the special enabling power of the Holy Spirit, [Footnote: Sermons. Patience, Section 13; Scripture Way of Salvation, Section 17; and Whedon on Mark 11: 24.]

All three locate the Divine efficiency before the declaration, "I believe that I receive," or "have received" (R. V.), making that declaration rest upon the perception of a Divine change within the consciousness. They all insist that saving faith is not a mere humanly moral exercise, but that power to believe with the heart descends from God, and that it must be waited for in prayer, and that it becomes in the believer a series of supernatural and spiritual acts, a habit of soul, at once the seed and fruit of the Divine life-stirring, uniting in itself the characters of penitent humility, self-renunciation, simple trust, and absolute obedience grounded in love. These teachers magnify the Divine element in faith. We look in vain in their writings for any such direction to a penitent as this, "Believe that you are saved, because, God says so in His Word," but rather believe that you are saved when you hear His Spirit crying, Abba, Father, in your heart.

Many modern teachers fall into the error of treating saving faith as an unaided intellectual act to be performed, at will, at any time. It is rather a spiritual act possible only when prompted by the Holy Spirit, who incites to faith only when He sees true repentance and a hearty surrender to God.

Then the Spirit reveals Christ and assists to grasp Him. In the refutation of the high predestinarian doctrine that faith is an irresistible grace sovereignly bestowed upon the elect, there is great danger of falling into the opposite error, called Pelagianism, which makes saving faith an exercise which the natural man is competent to put forth without the help of the Holy Spirit. The real guilt of unbelief lies in that voluntary indifference toward Christ, and impenitence of heart, in which the Holy Spirit cannot inspire saving faith.

In our introduction to " Aggressive Christianity ," we advertised, on behalf of the American churches, a universal want—Enthusiasm. In her brief Exeter-Hall address, Mrs. Booth discloses the source of the supply. Holiness is the well-spring of enthusiasm. Hence it is not a spring freshet, but an overflowing river of power in all its possessors, and, notably in the Salvation Army, bearing the unchurched masses of England on its bosom.

A holy enthusiasm is contagious and conquering. We cannot touch the people with the icicle of logic; but they will not fail to bow to the scepter of glowing and joyful love. Few men can reason; all can feel. Enthusiasm and full salvation, like the Siamese twins, cannot be separated and live.

The error of the modern pulpit is that of the blacksmith hammering cold steel—a faint impression and huge labor. The baptism of fire softening our assemblies would lighten the preacher's toil and multiply its productiveness.

The four addresses on Holiness are hortatory rather than argumentative or exegetical. They are spiritual cyclones. It is difficult to see how any Christian could withstand these impassioned appeals to make what Joseph Cook calls "an affectionate, total, irreversible, eternal, self-surrender to Jesus Christ, as both Saviour and Lord," in order to attain that "perfect similarity of feeling with God," wherein evangelical perfection consists.

It gives me great pleasure to have some humble part in echoing across the American continent these glowing utterances from the lips of this modern Deborah, the Christian prophetess raised up by God for the deliverance of His people from captivity to worldliness and religious apathy.

"Would God that all the Lord's people," men and women, "were prophets, and that the Lord would put His Spirit upon them!"

"Shall we the Spirit's course restrain, Or quench the heavenly fire?

Let God His messengers ordain, And whom He will inspire!

Blow as He list, the Spirit's choice Of instruments we bless: We will, if Christ be preached, rejoice, And wish the word success."

DANIEL STEELE.

Reading, Mass., Nov. 23, 1883.

fields.title: Repentance
fields.body_html:
Matthew 3:2 “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” Matthew 4:17 “From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.’” "Whereupon, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision: but shewed first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the regions of Judea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance."—ACTS 26. 19, 20.

In the mouths of three witnesses—John the Baptist, Jesus Christ, and the Apostle Paul—this word shall be established, namely, that repentance is an indispensable condition of entering the Kingdom of God.

People generally are quite confused on this subject, as though insisting that repentance were an arbitrary arrangement on the part of God. I believe God has made human salvation as easy as the Almighty, Infinite mind could make it. But there is a necessity in the case, that we should "repent and turn to God." It is just as necessary that my feelings be changed and brought to repentance towards God, as it is that the wicked, disobedient boy, should have his feelings brought back into harmony with his father before he can be forgiven. Precisely the same laws of mind are brought into action in both cases, and there is the same necessity in both.

If there is any father here who has a prodigal son, I ask, How is it that you are not reconciled to your son? You love him—love him intensely. Probably you are more conscious of your love for him than for any other of your children. Your heart yearns over him every day; you pray for him night and day; you dream of him by night; your heart yearns over your son, and you say, with David, "Absalom, Absalom, my son, my son." Why are you not reconciled? Why not pat him on the head, or stroke his face, and say, "My dear lad, I am well pleased with you. I love you with delight; I give you my approval?" Why are you always reproving him? Why are you obliged to hold him at arm's length? Why can you not live on friendly terms with him? Why can you not have him come in and out, and live with you on the same terms as the affectionate, obedient daughter?

"Oh!" you say, "the case is different; I cannot. It is not, 'I would not;' but, 'I cannot.'

Before that can possibly be, the boy's feelings must be changed towards me. He is at war with me; he has mistaken notions of me; he thinks I am hard, and cruel, and exacting, and severe. I have done all a father could do, but he sees things differently, to what they are, and has harbored these hard feelings against me until he hates me, and will go on in defiance of my will." You say, "It is a necessity that, as a wise and righteous father, I must insist on a change in him. I cannot receive him as a son, till he comes to my feet. He must confess his sin, and ask me to forgive him. Then, oh! how gladly will my fatherly affection gush out! How I should run to meet him, and put my arms around his neck! but there is a 'cannot' in the case." Just so. It is not that He does not love you, sinner; it is not that the great, benevolent heart of God has not, as it were, wept tears of blood over you; it is not that He would not put His loving arms around you this moment, if you would only come to His feet, and confess you were wrong, and seek His pardon; but, otherwise, He may not—He cannot.

The laws of His universe are against Him doing so. The good, it may be, of millions of immortal beings, is involved. He dare not, and He cannot, until there is a change of mind in you. You must repent. Luke 13:3 : “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” Well, if repentance be an indispensable condition of salvation, let us glance at it for a moment, and try to find out what repentance really is; and, oh! how full of confusion the world and the church are upon this subject!

I say it, because I know it by converse with hundreds of people. May the Holy Spirit help us! Well, first, repentance is not merely conviction of sin. Oh! if it only were, what a different world we should have tonight, for there are tens of thousands on whose hearts God's Spirit has done His office by convincing them of sin. I am afraid we should be perfectly alarmed, astounded, confounded, if we had any conception of the multitudes whom God has convinced of sin, as He did Agrippa and Festus. Oh! I could not tell you the numbers of people, who, in our anxious meetings, have grasped my hand, and said, "Oh! what would I give to feel as I once felt!

There was a time, fifteen, or seventeen, or twenty years ago," and so on, "when I was so deeply convinced of sin that I could scarcely sleep, or eat—that I could find no rest; but, instead of going on till I found peace, I got diverted, cooled down, and now, I feel as hard as a stone."

I am afraid there are tens of thousands in this condition—once convinced of sin. There are thousands of others, who are convinced now. They say, "Yes, it is true what the minister says. I know I ought to lay down the weapons of my warfare against God; I know I ought to cut off this right hand, and pluck out this right eye." They are convinced of sin, but they go no further. That is not repentance. They live this week as they did last. There is no response to the Spirit; they resist the Holy Spirit. Neither is repentance mere sorrow for sin. I have seen people weep bitterly, and writhe and struggle, but yet hug on to their idols, and in vain you try to shake them from them.

Oh! If Jesus Christ would have saved them with those idols, they would have no objection at all.

If they could have got through the narrow gate with this one particular idol, they would have gone through long since; but to part with that—that is another thing. Such people will weep like your stubborn child, when you want him to do something which he does not want to do. He will cry, and when you apply the rod he will cry harder, but he will not yield. When he yields, he becomes a penitent; but, until he does, he is merely a convicted sinner. When God applies the rod of His Spirit, the rod of His providence, the rod of His Word, sinners will cry, and wince, and whine, and make you believe they are praying, and want to be saved, but all the while they are holding their necks as stiff as iron. They will not submit. The moment they submit, they become true penitents, and get saved. There is no mistake more common than for people to suppose they are penitents when they are not. There are some of you in this condition, I know. I am afraid you are quite mistaken—you are not penitents.

God is true though every man should be a liar; and, if you had sought, as you say you have, and perhaps, think you have; if you had been sincere and honest with God, you would have been saved years ago. Oh! May God, the Holy Spirit, help you to come out and be HONEST. That is what God wants—that you be honest. "Oh," says He, "why cover ye my altar with tears, and bring your vain oblations? Just be honest, and I will be honest with you and bless you; but while you come before Me and weep and profess, and bring the halt, and the maimed, and the blind, a curse be upon you." He looks at you afar off. Be honest. Repentance is not mere sorrow for sin. You may be ever so sorry, and all the way down to death be hugging on to some forbidden possession, as was the young ruler. That is not repentance. Neither is repentance a promise that you will forsake sin in the future. Oh! If it were, there would be many penitents here tonight.

There is scarcely a poor drunkard that does not promise, in his own mind, or to his poor wife, or somebody, that he will give up his drinking. There is scarcely any kind of a sinner that does not continually promise that he will give up his sin, and serve God, but he does not do it. Then what is repentance?

Repentance is simply renouncing sin—turning round from darkness to light—from the power of Satan unto God. This is giving up sin in your heart, in purpose, in intention, in desire, resolving that you will give up every evil thing, and DO IT NOW. Of course, this involves sorrow, for how will any sane man turn himself round from a given course into another, if he does not repent having taken that course? It implies, also, hatred of, sin. He hates the course he formerly took, and turns round from it. He is like the prodigal, when he sat in the pigpen among the husks and the filth, he fully resolved, and at last he acts. He went, and that was the test of his penitence! He might have sat resolving and promising till now, if he had lived as long, and he would never have got the father's kiss, the father's welcome, if he had not started; but he went. He left the filth, the pigpen, the husks—he trampled them under his feet; he left the citizen of that country, and gave up all his subterfuges and excuses, and went to his father honestly, and said, "I have sinned!" which implied a great deal more in his language then than it does in ours now. "I have sinned against Heaven, and before thee;" and then comes the proof of his submission, "and am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants"—put me in a stable, or set me to clean the boots, so that I can be in thy family and have thy smile. That is repentance—Jesus Christ's own beautiful illustration of true penitence. Have you done that? Have you forsaken the accursed thing? Have you cut off that particular thing which the Holy Spirit has revealed to you?

Is the "but" the hindrance that keeps you out of the Kingdom? You know what it is, and you will never get saved until you renounce it. Submission is the test of penitence. My child may be willing to do a hundred and fifty other things, but, if he is not willing to submit on the one point of controversy, he is a rebel, and remains one until he yields. Now, here is just the difference between a spurious and a real repentance. I am afraid we have thousands in our churches who had a spurious repentance: they were convinced of sin—they were sorry for it; they wanted to live a better life, to love God in a sort of general way; but they skipped over the real point of controversy with God; they hid it from their pastor, perhaps, and from the deacons, and from the people who talked with them.

Now, I say, Abraham might have been willing to have given up every other thing that he possessed; but, if he had not been willing to give up Isaac, all else would have been useless. It is your Isaac God wants. You have got an Isaac, just as the young ruler had his possessions. You have got something that you are holding on to, that the Holy Spirit says you must let go, and you say, "I can't." Very well; then you must stop outside the kingdom. I beseech you, do not deceive yourselves by supposing that you repent, for you do not; but, oh! My dear friends, let me beseech you to repent.

The apostle says, "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men;" and this is, I believe, the greatest work of the ministry. To do what? To persuade men to submit. We are constantly talking to thousands of people who know just what God wants of them. We cannot bring many of them any new light or new Gospel. They know all about it. They used to tell me that so often, that I longed for a congregation of heathen, which I have found since then. Consequently, when they hear the Gospel, like the publicans and sinners of old, they go into the kingdom, while such as some of you who are the natural children of the kingdom, are shut out, because when they hear they receive, and submit, and obey, while you stand outside and hold on to your idols, and reason, and quibble, and reject! My dear friends, let me persuade you to trample under foot that idol, to tear down that refuge of lies, and to come to God honestly, and say, "Lord, here I am, to be a servant, to be nothing, to do anything, to suffer anything. I know I shall be happier with Thy smile and Thy blessing than all these evil things now make me without Thee."

When you come to a full surrender, my friends, you will get what you have been seeking, some of you, for years. But then another difficulty comes in, and people say, "I have not the power to repent." Oh! yes, you have. That is a grand mistake. You have the power, or God would not command it. You can repent. You can this moment lift up your eyes to Heaven, and say, with the prodigal, "Father, I have sinned, and I renounce my sin." You may not be able to weep—God nowhere requires or commands that; but you are able, this very moment, to renounce sin, in purpose, in resolution, in intention. Mind, don't confound the renouncing of the sin, with the power of saving yourself from it. If you renounce it, Jesus will come and save you from it. Like the man with the withered hand—Jesus intended to heal that man. Where was the power to come from to heal him? From Jesus, of course. The benevolence, the love, that prompted that healing, all came from Jesus; but Jesus wanted a condition. What was it? The response of the man's will; and so He said, "Stretch out your hand." If he had been like some of you, he would have said, "What an unreasonable command! You know I cannot do it—I cannot." Some of you say that; but I say you can, and you will have to do it, or you will be lost. What did Jesus want? He wanted that, "I will, Lord," inside the man—the response of his will. He wanted him to say, "Yes, Lord;" and, the moment he said that, Jesus supplied strength, and he stretched it forth, and you know what happened. Don't look forward, and say, "I shall not have strength;" that is not your matter—that is His. He will hold you up;—He is able, when you once commit yourself to Him. Now then, say, "I will." Never mind what you suffer—it shall be done. He will pour in the oil and balm. His glorious, blessed presence will do more for you in one hour, than all your struggling, praying, and wrestling have done all these weary years. He will lift you up out of the pit.

You are in the mire now, and the more you struggle the more you sink; but He will lift you out of it, and put your feet on the rock, and then you will stand firm. Stretch out your withered hand, whatever it may be;—say, "I will, Lord." You have the power, and mind, you have the obligation, which is universal and immediate. God "now command all men everywhere to repent," and to believe the Gospel. What a tyrant He must be if He commands that, and yet He knows you have not the power! Now, do you repent? Mind the old snare. Not, do you weep? The feeling will come after the surrender. Now, do not say, "I do not feel enough." Do you feel enough to be willing to forsake your sin? that is the point. He may deal with you as He dealt with those who repeatedly resisted Him before, of whom it is written: Hebrews 3:11 "As I swore in my wrath, ‘They shall not enter my rest.’"

Are you not provoking Him as they provoked Him?

For your own sake, be persuaded. For the peace, joy, strength, glory, and gladness that come from a life fully devoted to God and spent in service to others, yield to Him. But above all, submit because of His great love for you.

After a moment of hesitation, the man brushed away his tears, stood up, and followed him.

Will you come because of the deep longing with which your heavenly Father has pursued you all these years? For the sake of His love, will you come?

May the Lord help you.

Amen.
fields.body_text: Matthew 3:2 “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” Matthew 4:17 “From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.’” "Whereupon, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient unto the heavenly vision: but shewed first unto them of Damascus, and at Jerusalem, and throughout all the regions of Judea, and then to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, and do works meet for repentance."—ACTS 26. 19, 20. In the mouths of three witnesses—John the Baptist, Jesus Christ, and the Apostle Paul—this word shall be established, namely, that repentance is an indispensable condition of entering the Kingdom of God. People generally are quite confused on this subject, as though insisting that repentance were an arbitrary arrangement on the part of God. I believe God has made human salvation as easy as the Almighty, Infinite mind could make it. But there is a necessity in the case, that we should "repent and turn to God." It is just as necessary that my feelings be changed and brought to repentance towards God, as it is that the wicked, disobedient boy, should have his feelings brought back into harmony with his father before he can be forgiven. Precisely the same laws of mind are brought into action in both cases, and there is the same necessity in both. If there is any father here who has a prodigal son, I ask, How is it that you are not reconciled to your son? You love him—love him intensely. Probably you are more conscious of your love for him than for any other of your children. Your heart yearns over him every day; you pray for him night and day; you dream of him by night; your heart yearns over your son, and you say, with David, "Absalom, Absalom, my son, my son." Why are you not reconciled? Why not pat him on the head, or stroke his face, and say, "My dear lad, I am well pleased with you. I love you with delight; I give you my approval?" Why are you always reproving him? Why are you obliged to hold him at arm's length? Why can you not live on friendly terms with him? Why can you not have him come in and out, and live with you on the same terms as the affectionate, obedient daughter? "Oh!" you say, "the case is different; I cannot. It is not, 'I would not;' but, 'I cannot.' Before that can possibly be, the boy's feelings must be changed towards me. He is at war with me; he has mistaken notions of me; he thinks I am hard, and cruel, and exacting, and severe. I have done all a father could do, but he sees things differently, to what they are, and has harbored these hard feelings against me until he hates me, and will go on in defiance of my will." You say, "It is a necessity that, as a wise and righteous father, I must insist on a change in him. I cannot receive him as a son, till he comes to my feet. He must confess his sin, and ask me to forgive him. Then, oh! how gladly will my fatherly affection gush out! How I should run to meet him, and put my arms around his neck! but there is a 'cannot' in the case." Just so. It is not that He does not love you, sinner; it is not that the great, benevolent heart of God has not, as it were, wept tears of blood over you; it is not that He would not put His loving arms around you this moment, if you would only come to His feet, and confess you were wrong, and seek His pardon; but, otherwise, He may not—He cannot. The laws of His universe are against Him doing so. The good, it may be, of millions of immortal beings, is involved. He dare not, and He cannot, until there is a change of mind in you. You must repent. Luke 13:3 : “Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish.” Well, if repentance be an indispensable condition of salvation, let us glance at it for a moment, and try to find out what repentance really is; and, oh! how full of confusion the world and the church are upon this subject! I say it, because I know it by converse with hundreds of people. May the Holy Spirit help us! Well, first, repentance is not merely conviction of sin. Oh! if it only were, what a different world we should have tonight, for there are tens of thousands on whose hearts God's Spirit has done His office by convincing them of sin. I am afraid we should be perfectly alarmed, astounded, confounded, if we had any conception of the multitudes whom God has convinced of sin, as He did Agrippa and Festus. Oh! I could not tell you the numbers of people, who, in our anxious meetings, have grasped my hand, and said, "Oh! what would I give to feel as I once felt! There was a time, fifteen, or seventeen, or twenty years ago," and so on, "when I was so deeply convinced of sin that I could scarcely sleep, or eat—that I could find no rest; but, instead of going on till I found peace, I got diverted, cooled down, and now, I feel as hard as a stone." I am afraid there are tens of thousands in this condition—once convinced of sin. There are thousands of others, who are convinced now. They say, "Yes, it is true what the minister says. I know I ought to lay down the weapons of my warfare against God; I know I ought to cut off this right hand, and pluck out this right eye." They are convinced of sin, but they go no further. That is not repentance. They live this week as they did last. There is no response to the Spirit; they resist the Holy Spirit. Neither is repentance mere sorrow for sin. I have seen people weep bitterly, and writhe and struggle, but yet hug on to their idols, and in vain you try to shake them from them. Oh! If Jesus Christ would have saved them with those idols, they would have no objection at all. If they could have got through the narrow gate with this one particular idol, they would have gone through long since; but to part with that—that is another thing. Such people will weep like your stubborn child, when you want him to do something which he does not want to do. He will cry, and when you apply the rod he will cry harder, but he will not yield. When he yields, he becomes a penitent; but, until he does, he is merely a convicted sinner. When God applies the rod of His Spirit, the rod of His providence, the rod of His Word, sinners will cry, and wince, and whine, and make you believe they are praying, and want to be saved, but all the while they are holding their necks as stiff as iron. They will not submit. The moment they submit, they become true penitents, and get saved. There is no mistake more common than for people to suppose they are penitents when they are not. He looks at you afar off. Be honest. Repentance is not mere sorrow for sin. You may be ever so sorry, and all the way down to death be hugging on to some forbidden possession, as was the young ruler. That is not repentance. Neither is repentance a promise that you will forsake sin in the future. Oh! If it were, there would be many penitents here tonight. There is scarcely a poor drunkard that does not promise, in his own mind, or to his poor wife, or somebody, that he will give up his drinking. There is scarcely any kind of a sinner that does not continually promise that he will give up his sin, and serve God, but he does not do it. Then what is repentance? Repentance is simply renouncing sin—turning round from darkness to light—from the power of Satan unto God. This is giving up sin in your heart, in purpose, in intention, in desire, resolving that you will give up every evil thing, and DO IT NOW. Of course, this involves sorrow, for how will any sane man turn himself round from a given course into another, if he does not repent having taken that course? It implies, also, hatred of, sin. He hates the course he formerly took, and turns round from it. He is like the prodigal, when he sat in the pigpen among the husks and the filth, he fully resolved, and at last he acts. He went, and that was the test of his penitence! He might have sat resolving and promising till now, if he had lived as long, and he would never have got the father's kiss, the father's welcome, if he had not started; but he went. He left the filth, the pigpen, the husks—he trampled them under his feet; he left the citizen of that country, and gave up all his subterfuges and excuses, and went to his father honestly, and said, "I have sinned!" which implied a great deal more in his language then than it does in ours now. "I have sinned against Heaven, and before thee;" and then comes the proof of his submission, "and am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants"—put me in a stable, or set me to clean the boots, so that I can be in thy family and have thy smile. That is repentance—Jesus Christ's own beautiful illustration of true penitence. Have you done that? Have you forsaken the accursed thing? Have you cut off that particular thing which the Holy Spirit has revealed to you? Is the "but" the hindrance that keeps you out of the Kingdom? You know what it is, and you will never get saved until you renounce it. Submission is the test of penitence. My child may be willing to do a hundred and fifty other things, but, if he is not willing to submit on the one point of controversy, he is a rebel, and remains one until he yields. Now, here is just the difference between a spurious and a real repentance. I am afraid we have thousands in our churches who had a spurious repentance: they were convinced of sin—they were sorry for it; they wanted to live a better life, to love God in a sort of general way; but they skipped over the real point of controversy with God; they hid it from their pastor, perhaps, and from the deacons, and from the people who talked with them. Now, I say, Abraham might have been willing to have given up every other thing that he possessed; but, if he had not been willing to give up Isaac, all else would have been useless. It is your Isaac God wants. You have got an Isaac, just as the young ruler had his possessions. You have got something that you are holding on to, that the Holy Spirit says you must let go, and you say, "I can't." Very well; then you must stop outside the kingdom. I beseech you, do not deceive yourselves by supposing that you repent, for you do not; but, oh! My dear friends, let me beseech you to repent. The apostle says, "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men;" and this is, I believe, the greatest work of the ministry. To do what? To persuade men to submit. We are constantly talking to thousands of people who know just what God wants of them. We cannot bring many of them any new light or new Gospel. They know all about it. They used to tell me that so often, that I longed for a congregation of heathen, which I have found since then. Consequently, when they hear the Gospel, like the publicans and sinners of old, they go into the kingdom, while such as some of you who are the natural children of the kingdom, are shut out, because when they hear they receive, and submit, and obey, while you stand outside and hold on to your idols, and reason, and quibble, and reject! My dear friends, let me persuade you to trample under foot that idol, to tear down that refuge of lies, and to come to God honestly, and say, "Lord, here I am, to be a servant, to be nothing, to do anything, to suffer anything. I know I shall be happier with Thy smile and Thy blessing than all these evil things now make me without Thee." When you come to a full surrender, my friends, you will get what you have been seeking, some of you, for years. But then another difficulty comes in, and people say, "I have not the power to repent." Oh! yes, you have. That is a grand mistake. You have the power, or God would not command it. You can repent. You can this moment lift up your eyes to Heaven, and say, with the prodigal, "Father, I have sinned, and I renounce my sin." You may not be able to weep—God nowhere requires or commands that; but you are able, this very moment, to renounce sin, in purpose, in resolution, in intention. Mind, don't confound the renouncing of the sin, with the power of saving yourself from it. If you renounce it, Jesus will come and save you from it. Like the man with the withered hand—Jesus intended to heal that man. Where was the power to come from to heal him? From Jesus, of course. The benevolence, the love, that prompted that healing, all came from Jesus; but Jesus wanted a condition. What was it? The response of the man's will; and so He said, "Stretch out your hand." If he had been like some of you, he would have said, "What an unreasonable command! You know I cannot do it—I cannot." Some of you say that; but I say you can, and you will have to do it, or you will be lost. What did Jesus want? He wanted that, "I will, Lord," inside the man—the response of his will. He wanted him to say, "Yes, Lord;" and, the moment he said that, Jesus supplied strength, and he stretched it forth, and you know what happened. Don't look forward, and say, "I shall not have strength;" that is not your matter—that is His. He will hold you up;—He is able, when you once commit yourself to Him. Now then, say, "I will." Never mind what you suffer—it shall be done. He will pour in the oil and balm. His glorious, blessed presence will do more for you in one hour, than all your struggling, praying, and wrestling have done all these weary years. He will lift you up out of the pit. fields.title: Saving Faith
fields.body_html:
"Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?' And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'" Acts 16:30–31 This is one of the most misunderstood and misused texts in the Bible, and perhaps one that has been made to do as much work for the devil as for God. Let every believer present ask in faith for the light of the Holy Spirit as we seek to understand and apply it correctly. Let us consider: Who are to believe?

When are they to believe?

How are they to believe?

1. Who Are to Believe?

To whom does the Holy Spirit say, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved"? Notice carefully: not to all sinners indiscriminately.

Here is a serious mistake found in much of the teaching of our day. These words are often separated from their context and from many other passages that explain them. They are presented independently of the conditions that always accompanied them in the teaching and practice of the apostles. Indeed, it has only been within the last sixty or seventy years that this new approach has become common—preaching indiscriminately to unawakened, unconverted, and unrepentant sinners, "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ."

It seems to me that great harm has been done to the cause of Christ by this incorrect handling of the Word of God. Apart from being unscriptural, it is also unreasonable. How can an unawakened, unconvinced, and unrepentant sinner truly believe? One might as soon expect Satan to believe. It is impossible.

Thousands of such people say, "I do believe." Only a short time ago, my dear son was speaking with a man riding on top of an omnibus who was under the influence of alcohol and using very improper language. My son was trying to show him the danger of his sinful conduct as a transgressor of God's law. "Oh!" said the man, "it is not by works; it is by faith, and I believe as much as you do."

"Yes," replied my son, "but what do you believe?"

"Oh," he answered, "I believe in Jesus Christ, and of course I shall be saved."

That man is a sample of thousands. I meet such people every day.

They believe there was a man named Jesus, and that He died for sinners—even for them. But regarding the exercise of saving faith, they know no more about it than Agrippa or Felix. This becomes evident when they come near death. Then these same people wring their hands, despair, and call for Christians to come and pray with them.

If they had truly believed, why all this fear and alarm at the approach of death? They were believers only in the mind, not in the heart. They accepted the facts recorded in Scripture, but they did not believe in the biblical sense of the word. If they had, their faith would have saved them. We maintain that it is both useless and unscriptural to preach "only believe" to such people.

Christians have not fulfilled their responsibility when they simply tell sinners that Jesus died for them and that they should believe in Him. They have a more difficult task: to help open their eyes to their true condition, so that by the power of the Spirit they realise they are sinners in need of salvation.

When people recognise that they are spiritually sick, they will run to the Great Physician. The eyes of the soul must be opened to the reality of sin and to the consequences of sin. This realisation should create an earnest desire to be saved from it. God's great instrument for accomplishing this is His law, which serves as a schoolmaster leading sinners to Christ as their Savior.

There is not one case in the New Testament where the apostles urged people to believe, or where a person is described as believing, without good reason to conclude that conviction of sin and repentance had already taken place.

The one apparent exception is Simon the sorcerer.

Like many people in times of powerful religious movements, Simon was carried along by the influence of the meetings and by the example of those around him. He professed faith.

No doubt he accepted the fact that Jesus died on the cross. He received the facts of Christianity into his mind and, in that sense, became a believer—just as tens of thousands do today. He was even baptised. But when the testing point came—whether his own interests or God's interests mattered most to him—his true condition became clear.

As the apostle said: "Your heart is not right before God." Acts 8:21 No one is converted whose heart is not right with God. That is the test.

If Simon had truly been converted, his heart would have been right with God, and he would never have imagined that the gift of the Holy Spirit could be purchased with money. Peter went on to say: "For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity." Acts 8:23 And what did he say next?

Did he say, "Believe immediately"?

No.

Instead he said: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you."

Repent first, and then receive forgiveness.

Thus, we receive a double lesson from this passage.

Simon is the only recorded case of someone professing belief where there is not clear evidence in the passage itself that conviction and repentance preceded faith. Yet even here, the outcome proves the point.

Simon possessed the faith of the mind, but not the faith of the heart. Therefore, his profession ended in failure and despair. Some have written to me this week saying that they had believed.

They had been persuaded into making a profession of faith, but no fruit followed.

Ah, it was not heart faith. It was merely intellectual faith—like Simon's. It left you worse than it found you, and ever since you have been struggling and wandering in spiritual darkness.

But do not conclude that this was genuine faith and that genuine faith has failed. Rather, take courage and begin again. Repent, and seek the real thing.

Satan always provides a counterfeit. Therefore, do not fall into despair because the wrong kind of faith did not succeed. That failure does not make God's true faith ineffective. Certainly not!

Consider another example—the three thousand converted in a single day. Surely this is a biblical illustration. No one can call it anti-gospel or legalistic.

What was the first thing Peter did?

He drove the penetrating truth of God into their hearts and brought them under conviction.

He awakened them to the seriousness of their condition until they cried out: "Brothers, what shall we do?" Acts 2:37 They were deeply troubled. Their hearts were pierced. Their eyes were opened to the terrible consequences of their sin.

As a result, they cried out before the great crowd, seeking the way of salvation.

Peter first convinced them of sin, and in doing so followed God's appointed order.

Again, the eunuch is often quoted as an illustration of faith; but what state of mind was he in? Was he a careless, unconvicted sinner? There he was—an Ethiopian, a heathen; but where had he been?

To Jerusalem, to worship the true and living God in the best way he knew and according to the understanding he had. Then, what was he doing when Philip found him? He was not content with merely worshiping at the temple and then going back to his ordinary life without concern. He was searching the Scriptures. He was honestly seeking after God, and the Holy Spirit always knows where such souls are. So He said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” There is a man seeking after Me; there is a man whose heart is sincerely set on finding Me. Go and preach Christ, and tell him to believe. That man would have sacrificed, done, or lost anything for salvation, and as soon as Philip explained the way of faith, he received it, of course, as all such souls will.

Saul, on his way to Damascus, is another example. Jesus Christ Himself was the preacher there, and surely He could not be mistaken. His method was perfect. Where did He begin? What did He say to Saul? He saw an honest-hearted man. Saul was sincere, as far as he understood, and if in any case there seemed to be a need for the immediate reception of Christ by faith, it was in his.

But the Lord Jesus Christ did not say one word about faith. “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4, ESV)—tearing away the bandages of deception from his eyes and letting him see the wickedness of his conduct.

When Saul said, “Who are you, Lord?” (Acts 9:5, ESV), He repeated the accusation. He did not come with words of comfort. He did not immediately heal the wound; but He said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9:5, ESV). He pressed the truth even deeper, opening Saul’s eyes wider and making him more aware of his guilt. Then He sent him on to Damascus, where he spent three days before receiving healing. God sent a humble human instrument to him, and Saul had to hear and obey his words before the scales fell from his eyes, before the assurance of forgiveness came, and before the Holy Spirit filled his soul.

I wonder what Paul was doing during those three days! Not singing songs of thanksgiving and praise. That would come later. What do you think he was doing? He neither ate nor drank, and he remained in darkness. What was he doing? No doubt he was praying. No doubt he was seeking after this Christ who had spoken to him on the road. No doubt he was looking with horror upon his past life and renouncing forever his opposition to Jesus Christ and His Gospel.

Of course, he was bringing forth fruits worthy of repentance, according to the divine order (Acts 26). Then Ananias came and preached Christ to him. He believed unto salvation, the scales fell from his eyes, and his mouth was filled with praise and thanksgiving to God.

Cornelius is another example, but what was the state of his mind and heart? We know that he feared God and practiced righteousness as far as he was able. He gave generously to the people and prayed continually. That is more than some of you have ever done, even though you live in Gospel times. You have never spent a whole night praying about your soul—not even half a night, some of you. Cornelius did. He was seeking God. He sincerely wanted to know Him. He was willing, whatever the cost, to do His will. Consequently, the Lord sent him the glorious message of the revelation of Jesus Christ.

I could continue giving examples, but I must stop. We have said enough to show who are to believe: truly repentant sinners, and they only.

This text is addressed to a repenting, enlightened, convicted sinner. Some of you are enlightened, convinced, and so troubled that you cannot sleep. You do repent. You are the very people, then, to whom this text comes: Believe. You are in the very condition of the jailer.

“Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31, ESV). Now let us consider the state of mind the jailer was in. We see from the whole account how his eyes had been opened. The earthquake had done that. Some people need an earthquake before their eyes are opened, and it has to be a powerful one. The jailer’s eyes were opened, and he made the best use of the opportunity.

A short time before, he had been cruelly treating the apostles. Talk about a change—here was a change.

Then he cried out, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (Acts 16:30, ESV). In effect, he was saying, “I am ready to do anything; just tell me what.” When a soul comes to that state of mind, there is nothing more to do but believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. He came trembling, fell before them, and afterward washed their wounds. When you reach that state of mind, you will soon be saved. You will have nothing more to do but believe. You will find it easy then.

2. When is a Sinner to Believe?

When he repents.

Here again I am going to answer some of your letters. One person writes: “I am afraid I do not realise my sin sufficiently. I have no particular agony on account of sin, but I do see my whole life as one huge error and sin.”

Nothing is more common than for people to deceive themselves on this point. That person is confusing feeling with conviction. He thinks that because he has not experienced the extreme agony that some have, he is therefore not sufficiently convinced of sin. Yet the Holy Spirit has opened his eyes to see that his whole life has been one great error and sin. He is convinced that it has all been sin—not merely isolated sins here and there, separated from the rest of his life, but a perception of his true condition that causes him to see his whole life as sinful.

Surely, my friend, you are convinced. Who but the Holy Spirit could have shown you that? Now, the truly repentant soul first sees sin; second, hates sin; third, renounces sin.

Let me test you by each of these marks. Do not let Satan deceive you and cause you to deny what God has been doing in your heart. Face the facts. When you have reached a conclusion, do not allow him to start an argument in your mind. Hold firmly to what you know to be true and move forward from there, or you will never find peace. Satan is the accuser of the brethren—and, I suppose, of the sisters too.

I will be as honest and searching with you as I can. I will not avoid the examination, but once we have examined and found the truth, stand upon it for Christ’s sake, and do not let it slip from beneath your feet. Satan will try to rob you of your common sense, your conscience, and your convictions.

You see sin. A completely unawakened soul does not see sin in its true character, its seriousness, or its consequences. Such a person admits that all people are sinners. Oh yes, but he does not see the deadly and condemning nature of sin. He does not see what an evil and bitter thing sin is in itself.

Now, only the Holy Spirit can open a person’s eyes to see this. Without Him, all my preaching— or anyone else’s preaching—even the preaching of angels, if they were allowed to preach, could continue forever and never bring conviction of sin. If you see sin, it is the Holy Spirit who has opened your eyes. Thank Him and take courage, my friend. If God has dealt with you this far and opened your eyes to see the character and consequences of sin, does it not suggest that He also desires to save you from it? He has opened your eyes so that He may anoint them with eye salve and enable you to see light in His light.

Now, have you come this far? You have told me that your life has been one great sin. Others speak of one particular sin. Whatever it may be, if you are convicted of sin, it is the Holy Spirit who has convicted you. Therefore, thank God and take courage this far.

Further, the true penitent hates sin; that is, his attitude toward sin is completely different from what it was before. There was a time when you could commit sin almost without noticing it or feeling concern. People often do not realise the great change that has taken place in them in this respect because they are brought to it gradually.

Think back to your unawakened state. How did you live then? The very things that now cause you such distress were things you practiced every day without concern. The things that now horrify you, even in thought or temptation, were once part of your daily life without any sense of guilt.

You had no hatred of sin and no fear of it. You were a willing slave of Satan. Now you are an unwilling one. Then you ran toward sin; now he has to drive you toward it. When you fall, it is against your will. You hate sin.

Now, this does not mean you are already saved from it. Nor does it mean that you have the power to save yourself from it. In fact, this is the very struggle the apostle describes when portraying the unsuccessful efforts of a convicted sinner. The things you do not want to do, you find yourself doing; and the things you desire to do, you lack the power to accomplish. Nevertheless, you desire to do what is right. That is the difference.

Once, you had no desire to do those things. In fact, you may even have thought that those who did were hypocrites. Now, you feel very differently. You struggle, strive, pray, and stay watchful.

Some of you have told me so, and yet you say, “I am overcome again and again.”

Of course you are, because you are not yet saved. But do you not see that you desire to be? You hate the sin that holds you captive. You struggle against it. You watch against it. Perhaps you are not overcome nearly as often as before.

People do not realise how much they owe to the convicting and restraining power of the Holy Spirit, who helps their weakness even now, enabling them to cut off the right hand and pluck out the right eye, and bringing them into a waiting attitude before God, like Cornelius and the eunuch.

Some of you, my hearers, are seeking after God. You long for deliverance and are striving against sin.

Take another illustration. I do not mean that the soul has power to save itself from its inward corruption. That is what Jesus Christ gives when He saves. But consider this: here is a man who is addicted to drink. He is a drunkard. Then he becomes convicted of sin. The Spirit of God says to him, “Will you give up the cup?” Then the struggle begins.

Now, should that man be taught to continue drinking and simply expect God to save him? Should you keep telling him, “Never mind the drink; just believe on the Lord Jesus Christ and you will be saved”? Or should you tell him, “You must put away your sin. Cut off that right hand. Pluck out that right eye. Renounce that drink forever in your heart, purpose, and will. Until you do so, you cannot truly exercise faith in the Lord Jesus”?

Here is another person who is addicted to lying. When he is convicted of sin, he begins to guard his lips so that he may not sin with his mouth. He succeeds to some extent, or rather, the Holy Spirit helps him succeed, so that he does not lie as he once did. He still fails from time to time because he has not yet found full power over it, but he is firmly determined, and as far as his will is concerned, he is cutting off this outward sin and waiting in obedience for complete deliverance and salvation.

There is also the servant who regularly steals from his master's cash box. He attends a religious meeting and becomes convicted. Then the Spirit of God says, “You must stop that dishonesty. You cannot come to this meeting night after night, claiming to want salvation, while every day you continue stealing from your master. You must cut off that right hand. Give up that theft. Resolve to make restitution, and wait before Me while bringing forth fruits worthy of repentance.”

You see what I mean. Some of you are in exactly that position—you know you are. Whatever sinful habit may have hold of you, the principle is the same. Jesus Christ wants you to renounce that habit in your will, determination, and purpose. You do not have the power to free yourself from it. You may struggle, as some of you say you are doing, but it still overcomes you. He knows all about that. Yet He approves of the struggle, the effort, the watchfulness, and the determination.

When He saves you, He will give you the power, and then you will stand instead of falling, because He Himself will uphold you.

Now you know that you have come this far. You know that if you had the power right now to completely destroy the hold of that evil habit over your life forever, you would do it without a moment's hesitation. You say, “Oh yes, I would. If only I had the power.” That is repentance. That is genuine repentance.

What you cannot do for yourself, Christ meets you where you are and says, “I will do it for you. I will break the power of that habit. I will deliver you from the hand of the enemy. I will free you from that bondage. Only place your faith in Me, and I will lift you up. I will fill you with My Spirit.

You shall stand in Me and by Me, and what you are now struggling to do for yourself, I will do for you.”

Then you have come this far—that you hate sin?

“Yes, I do.”

You have written it in your letters to me, and others are saying it who have not written.

“Yes,” you say, “I desire to be saved from it. If I could save myself from sin this very moment and never sin again, I would do so.”

Would you? Is that not repentance? What else could it be?

Suppose you had a disobedient and rebellious son. He had lived in defiance of your authority, wasted your money, and trampled your commands underfoot. Then suppose he comes to see the error of his ways. Perhaps suffering opened his eyes. Perhaps poverty did. Perhaps it was something else. In any case, he sees it.

He comes home and says: “Father, what a fool I have been. How wicked I have been. I see it all now. I did not see it when I was doing it. I see my sinful course, the sins that caused you grief and brought sorrow to your life. Oh, how I hate it all. I repent in dust and ashes. Father, I forsake it all. I come home to you.”

What would you say?

Would you say, “My son, you have not repented enough. Go away and come back when you feel more sorrow”?

No. Your father's heart would reach out in love and forgiveness. You would embrace him and welcome him home.

“Just so, I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:10, ESV).

There would be joy in that family over the return of the wandering child.

But suppose the son said: “Father, I truly repent and forsake my sins, but there are companions who may influence me again, and there are habits so powerful that I fear they may overcome me. Let me stay close to you. I need your strength.”

What would you say?

Would you not answer: “Then come in, my son. Stay with me, and I will protect you. I will help you. You shall not walk alone. I will be with you and uphold you.”

As far as any human father could protect another, you would protect your son. He would never lack your sympathy or support, day or night.

Your heavenly Father lacks neither sympathy nor strength. His eye never sleeps. His arm never grows weary. You need only bring your helpless weakness to His almighty strength through this act of faith, and He will uphold you, even if a legion of devils surrounds you.

Lastly, you renounce your sins—that is, in your will, purpose, and determination.

You say, “I never want to grieve Him again.”

You sing it, and you mean it.

“I do not want to grieve Him anymore.”

If you could live without grieving Him, you would count every sacrifice worthwhile. Is that not repentance? You know it is.

You renounce sin. You do not say, “Lord Jesus, save me while I hold on to this right hand and this right eye. Save me while I cling to these forbidden things.”

No.

You say, “Lord Jesus, save me from them. Make me clean.”

That is repentance. You see sin. You hate sin. You renounce sin.

Now then, believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Oh, Holy Spirit, reveal the simple way of faith.

You ask, “How am I to believe?”

A troubled soul once asked me this question in large letters: “How am I to believe?”

How does a bride believe in her husband when she gives herself to him at the marriage altar? She entrusts herself to him. She believes in him. She enters into a covenant with him and then goes home and lives as though that covenant is true.

That is faith.

How do you trust a physician when you are sick and lying on your bed, whether in peace or suffering? You place your case in his hands. You commit yourself to his care. You trust his skill and follow his instructions.

Have faith like this in Jesus Christ.

Trust and obey, and expect that it will be with you according to His Word.

Instead, the faith of many people is like that of a person suffering from a serious illness. A friend tells him about a wonderful physician who has cured hundreds of similar cases and provides abundant evidence that the doctor is both able and willing to heal him if he will only place himself under his care. The sick man may completely believe his friend's testimony about the physician, yet for some hidden reason he refuses to entrust himself to him.

Many people treat Jesus Christ in the same way. They believe He can heal the disease of sin on His appointed terms. They believe that He shows no partiality. They believe that He has saved hundreds who were just as sinful as they are. Yet for some reason they do not trust Him. They hold back.

What you need to do is place your case in His hands and say: “Lord Jesus, I come as You have invited me, confessing and forsaking my sin. If I could, I would leave it behind forever this very moment. You know that I come renouncing it, yet without the power to save myself from it. And now, Lord Jesus, You have said, ‘Whoever comes to me I will never cast out’” (John 6:37, ESV).

“I do come. You do not cast me out. You receive me. Blessed Heavenly Father, I give myself to You. I place my sins upon the sacrifice of Your Son. You have said that You will receive me and forgive me for His sake. Now I roll my guilty burden onto Him, and I believe Your promise. I trust You to be true to Your Word.”

That is faith.

“But,” said a dear lady, “I do not feel it.”

No. You must trust first.

Notice carefully: you are not first to believe that you are saved, but to believe that He is saving you now according to His promise.

“Whatsoever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours” (Mark 11:24, ESV).

That is the principle of faith. Believe that you receive before you feel. When you receive, then you will feel. God will prove true, and every person or devil who contradicts Him will be found a liar.

Throw your arms around the Crucified One. Take hold of the hand of the Son of God. Bring your guilty soul to the foot of His cross and say: “You receive me. You forgive me. You cleanse me. You save me.”

Keep speaking the language of faith.

I have seen many souls enter into freedom while repeating these precious words personally: “He was wounded for my transgressions; he was crushed for my iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought me peace, and with his stripes I am healed” (Isaiah 53:5, ESV).

Keep speaking the language of faith all the way home tonight.

Go into your room and say: “I am determined to be saved, if salvation is truly offered to me.”

Resolve that if you perish, you will perish there at the foot of the cross, pleading for mercy. But you will not perish, for He has promised mercy to those who come.

I have never known a soul to come to this point and not soon find salvation.

Get into the lifeboat. Leave behind the wreck of your own righteousness and your own efforts.

Step fully into the lifeboat of Christ's sacrifice. Hold firmly to Him, and determine never to let go until the Spirit bears witness within your soul, crying, “Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15, ESV), and you know with certainty that you have passed from death to life (John 5:24, ESV).

May the Lord help you.

Amen.
fields.body_text: "Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?' And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'" Acts 16:30–31 This is one of the most misunderstood and misused texts in the Bible, and perhaps one that has been made to do as much work for the devil as for God. Let every believer present ask in faith for the light of the Holy Spirit as we seek to understand and apply it correctly. Let us consider: Who are to believe? When are they to believe? How are they to believe? 1. Who Are to Believe? To whom does the Holy Spirit say, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved"? Notice carefully: not to all sinners indiscriminately. Here is a serious mistake found in much of the teaching of our day. These words are often separated from their context and from many other passages that explain them. They are presented independently of the conditions that always accompanied them in the teaching and practice of the apostles. Indeed, it has only been within the last sixty or seventy years that this new approach has become common—preaching indiscriminately to unawakened, unconverted, and unrepentant sinners, "Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ." It seems to me that great harm has been done to the cause of Christ by this incorrect handling of the Word of God. Apart from being unscriptural, it is also unreasonable. How can an unawakened, unconvinced, and unrepentant sinner truly believe? One might as soon expect Satan to believe. It is impossible. Thousands of such people say, "I do believe." Only a short time ago, my dear son was speaking with a man riding on top of an omnibus who was under the influence of alcohol and using very improper language. My son was trying to show him the danger of his sinful conduct as a transgressor of God's law. "Oh!" said the man, "it is not by works; it is by faith, and I believe as much as you do." "Yes," replied my son, "but what do you believe?" "Oh," he answered, "I believe in Jesus Christ, and of course I shall be saved." That man is a sample of thousands. I meet such people every day. They believe there was a man named Jesus, and that He died for sinners—even for them. But regarding the exercise of saving faith, they know no more about it than Agrippa or Felix. This becomes evident when they come near death. Then these same people wring their hands, despair, and call for Christians to come and pray with them. If they had truly believed, why all this fear and alarm at the approach of death? They were believers only in the mind, not in the heart. They accepted the facts recorded in Scripture, but they did not believe in the biblical sense of the word. If they had, their faith would have saved them. We maintain that it is both useless and unscriptural to preach "only believe" to such people. Christians have not fulfilled their responsibility when they simply tell sinners that Jesus died for them and that they should believe in Him. They have a more difficult task: to help open their eyes to their true condition, so that by the power of the Spirit they realise they are sinners in need of salvation. When people recognise that they are spiritually sick, they will run to the Great Physician. The eyes of the soul must be opened to the reality of sin and to the consequences of sin. This realisation should create an earnest desire to be saved from it. God's great instrument for accomplishing this is His law, which serves as a schoolmaster leading sinners to Christ as their Savior. There is not one case in the New Testament where the apostles urged people to believe, or where a person is described as believing, without good reason to conclude that conviction of sin and repentance had already taken place. The one apparent exception is Simon the sorcerer. Like many people in times of powerful religious movements, Simon was carried along by the influence of the meetings and by the example of those around him. He professed faith. No doubt he accepted the fact that Jesus died on the cross. He received the facts of Christianity into his mind and, in that sense, became a believer—just as tens of thousands do today. He was even baptised. But when the testing point came—whether his own interests or God's interests mattered most to him—his true condition became clear. As the apostle said: "Your heart is not right before God." Acts 8:21 No one is converted whose heart is not right with God. That is the test. If Simon had truly been converted, his heart would have been right with God, and he would never have imagined that the gift of the Holy Spirit could be purchased with money. Peter went on to say: "For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity." Acts 8:23 And what did he say next? Did he say, "Believe immediately"? No. Instead he said: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you." Repent first, and then receive forgiveness. Thus, we receive a double lesson from this passage. Simon is the only recorded case of someone professing belief where there is not clear evidence in the passage itself that conviction and repentance preceded faith. Yet even here, the outcome proves the point. Simon possessed the faith of the mind, but not the faith of the heart. Therefore, his profession ended in failure and despair. Some have written to me this week saying that they had believed. They had been persuaded into making a profession of faith, but no fruit followed. Ah, it was not heart faith. It was merely intellectual faith—like Simon's. It left you worse than it found you, and ever since you have been struggling and wandering in spiritual darkness. But do not conclude that this was genuine faith and that genuine faith has failed. Rather, take courage and begin again. Repent, and seek the real thing. Satan always provides a counterfeit. Therefore, do not fall into despair because the wrong kind of faith did not succeed. That failure does not make God's true faith ineffective. Certainly not! Consider another example—the three thousand converted in a single day. Surely this is a biblical illustration. No one can call it anti-gospel or legalistic. What was the first thing Peter did? He drove the penetrating truth of God into their hearts and brought them under conviction. He awakened them to the seriousness of their condition until they cried out: "Brothers, what shall we do?" Acts 2:37 They were deeply troubled. Their hearts were pierced. Their eyes were opened to the terrible consequences of their sin. As a result, they cried out before the great crowd, seeking the way of salvation. Peter first convinced them of sin, and in doing so followed God's appointed order. Again, the eunuch is often quoted as an illustration of faith; but what state of mind was he in? Was he a careless, unconvicted sinner? There he was—an Ethiopian, a heathen; but where had he been? To Jerusalem, to worship the true and living God in the best way he knew and according to the understanding he had. Then, what was he doing when Philip found him? He was not content with merely worshiping at the temple and then going back to his ordinary life without concern. He was searching the Scriptures. He was honestly seeking after God, and the Holy Spirit always knows where such souls are. So He said to Philip, “Go over and join this chariot.” There is a man seeking after Me; there is a man whose heart is sincerely set on finding Me. Go and preach Christ, and tell him to believe. That man would have sacrificed, done, or lost anything for salvation, and as soon as Philip explained the way of faith, he received it, of course, as all such souls will. Saul, on his way to Damascus, is another example. Jesus Christ Himself was the preacher there, and surely He could not be mistaken. His method was perfect. Where did He begin? What did He say to Saul? He saw an honest-hearted man. Saul was sincere, as far as he understood, and if in any case there seemed to be a need for the immediate reception of Christ by faith, it was in his. But the Lord Jesus Christ did not say one word about faith. “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4, ESV)—tearing away the bandages of deception from his eyes and letting him see the wickedness of his conduct. When Saul said, “Who are you, Lord?” (Acts 9:5, ESV), He repeated the accusation. He did not come with words of comfort. He did not immediately heal the wound; but He said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting” (Acts 9:5, ESV). He pressed the truth even deeper, opening Saul’s eyes wider and making him more aware of his guilt. Then He sent him on to Damascus, where he spent three days before receiving healing. God sent a humble human instrument to him, and Saul had to hear and obey his words before the scales fell from his eyes, before the assurance of forgiveness came, and before the Holy Spirit filled his soul. I wonder what Paul was doing during those three days! Not singing songs of thanksgiving and praise. That would come later. What do you think he was doing? He neither ate nor drank, and he remained in darkness. What was he doing? No doubt he was praying. No doubt he was seeking after this Christ who had spoken to him on the road. No doubt he was looking with horror upon his past life and renouncing forever his opposition to Jesus Christ and His Gospel. Of course, he was bringing forth fruits worthy of repentance, according to the divine order (Acts 26). Then Ananias came and preached Christ to him. He believed unto salvation, the scales fell from his eyes, and his mouth was filled with praise and thanksgiving to God. Cornelius is another example, but what was the state of his mind and heart? We know that he feared God and practiced righteousness as far as he was able. He gave generously to the people and prayed continually. That is more than some of you have ever done, even though you live in Gospel times. You have never spent a whole night praying about your soul—not even half a night, some of you. Cornelius did. He was seeking God. He sincerely wanted to know Him. He was willing, whatever the cost, to do His will. Consequently, the Lord sent him the glorious message of the revelation of Jesus Christ. I could continue giving examples, but I must stop. We have said enough to show who are to believe: truly repentant sinners, and they only. This text is addressed to a repenting, enlightened, convicted sinner. Some of you are enlightened, convinced, and so troubled that you cannot sleep. You do repent. You are the very people, then, to whom this text comes: Believe. You are in the very condition of the jailer. “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved” (Acts 16:31, ESV). Now let us consider the state of mind the jailer was in. We see from the whole account how his eyes had been opened. The earthquake had done that. Some people need an earthquake before their eyes are opened, and it has to be a powerful one. The jailer’s eyes were opened, and he made the best use of the opportunity. A short time before, he had been cruelly treating the apostles. Talk about a change—here was a change. Then he cried out, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” (Acts 16:30, ESV). In effect, he was saying, “I am ready to do anything; just tell me what.” When a soul comes to that state of mind, there is nothing more to do but believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. He came trembling, fell before them, and afterward washed their wounds. When you reach that state of mind, you will soon be saved. You will have nothing more to do but believe.
